newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Mother Teresa calls for peace in homeland Albania.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa calls for peace in homeland Albania.

text.p: Albania's most famous citizen, Mother Teresa, on Thursday appealed for peace in her homeland, saying the violence in the Balkan state was causing her great pain.

The frail Nobel Peace Prize winner called for an end to the chaos, caused by the collapse of get-rich-quick "pyramid" funds, in which at least 300 people have been killed and more than 700 wounded since February.

"The news of the turmoil enveloping our beautiful country has caused me great pain," Mother Teresa wrote in a letter addressed to the Albanian people, published in daily newspaper Rilindja Demockratike.
"You know how much I love Albania. I have visited it often. I am hearing with great pain of lost lives and people wounded during violence.
"I understand the pain of those who lost money but would plead with you to stop causing each other more suffering."
Many of Albania's 3.4 million people have ploughed their life savings into pyramid schemes since the collapse of communism in 1990, lured by the promise of returns of up to 50 percent a month.
But when five of the country's nine pyramid funds collapsed in January this year, angry depositors blamed the government and the country slid into near-anarchy.

An eight-nation United Nations peacekeeping force of 6,000 soldiers is fanning across the country to ensure food and medical supplies reach hospitals, orphanages and the worst affected people in Albania, Europe's poorest country.
Armed rebels still control much of the south. They are demanding the resignation of right-wing President Sali Berisha whom they blame for the collapse of the schemes.
Mother Teresa, born in 1910 to Albanian parents in Skopje in Macedonia and christened Gonxhe Bojaxhi, said she was praying for her fellow Albanians.

"Mother is praying very much for all my precious people of Albania so that everyone can learn to love till the point of pain and in this way we can bring peace to the country and every heart," she wrote.

Author Ismail Kadare, arguably Albania's second most well-known citizen, dismissed any speculation that the crisis in Albania was a feud between the country's mountainous northern region and the more prosperous south.

Kadare, 59, who has been shortlisted several times for the Nobel literature prize, told daily newspaper The Albania that foreign media were continuing to push this view to the detriment of his country, which had no ethnic or religious conflicts.
"For months on end the press spoke about the war that would erupt between the north and the south, a problem that has never existed in Albania," said Kadare, who has lived in France since 1989.
"But the media wanted blood to feed its advertising. And so the Albanians started to torch their own country."
